props.title: 21 Grams

sections.content: 21 Grams revolutionized non-linear storytelling through its intricate web of interconnected tragedies. Director Alejandro González Iñárritu crafted a devastating exploration of grief, redemption, and chance encounters that influenced countless films that followed. Like Memento (2000), it proves that fragmenting chronology isn't just a gimmick - it's a powerful tool for examining how trauma shapes memory and perception. The raw performances from Sean Penn, Naomi Watts, and Benicio Del Toro set a new standard for emotional authenticity in ensemble dramas.

sections.content: Iñárritu's signature multi-narrative style reached its apex with 21 Grams, building on techniques he developed in Amores Perros (2000). The film's title refers to the supposed weight lost at the moment of death, but it's really about the crushing weight of living. The director would continue exploring interconnected destinies in Babel (2006) and Biutiful (2010), but never with quite the same devastating intimacy as this breakthrough work.

The film's influence extends beyond just narrative structure. Its gritty, handheld cinematography by Rodrigo Prieto inspired a generation of indie dramas. The approach was later refined in films like Crash (2004) and Syriana (2005), though few matched 21 Grams' emotional intensity. The film also marked a turning point for Hollywood's embrace of Mexican filmmakers, paving the way for Alfonso Cuarón and Guillermo del Toro's later successes. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Drama

While 21 Grams shares DNA with earlier non-linear films like Pulp Fiction (1994), it pioneered a more emotionally-driven approach to fractured storytelling. Later films like The Hours (2002) and Babel (2006) would adopt similar techniques to explore interconnected lives, but few achieved the same raw power. The film's unflinching look at grief and redemption influenced everything from Manchester by the Sea (2016) to Moonlight (2016).
